stanzas: अयिगिरिनन्दिनि नन्दितमेदिनि विश्वविनोदिनि नन्दनुते गिरिवरविन्ध्य-शिरोधिनिवासिनि विष्णुविलासिनि जिष्णुनुते।
भगवति हे शितिकण्ठकुटुम्बिनि भूरिकुटुम्बिनि भूरिकृते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१॥
सुरवरवर्षिणि दुर्धरधर्षिणि दुर्मुखमर्षिणी हर्षरते त्रिभुवनपोषिणि शंकरतोषिणि किल्बिषमोषिणि घोषरते।
दनुजनिरोषिणि दितिसुतरोषिणि दुर्मदशोषिणि सिन्धुसुते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥२॥
अयि जगदम्ब मदम्ब कदम्बवनप्रियवासिनि हासरते शिखरिशिरोमणि तुङ्गहिमालयशृङ्गनिजालयमध्यगते।
मधुमधुरे मधुकैटभगञ्जिनि कैटभभञ्जिनि रासरते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥३॥
अयि शतखण्डविखण्डितरुण्डवितुण्डितशुण्डगजाधिपते रिपुगजगण्डविदारणचण्डपराक्रमशुण्डमृगाधिपते।
निजभुजदण्डनिपातितखण्डविपातितमुण्डभटाधिपते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥४॥
अयि रणदुर्मदशत्रुवधोद्यतदुर्धरनिर्जरशक्तिभृते चतुरविचारधुरीणमहाशिवदूतकृतप्रमथाधिपते।
दुरितदुरीहदुराशयदुर्मतिदानवदूतकृतान्तमते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥५॥
अयि शरणागतवैरिवधूवरवीरवराभयदानकरे त्रिभुवनमस्तकशूलविरोधिशिरोधिकृतामलशूलकरे।
दुमिदुमितामरदुन्दुभिनादमहो मुखरीकृततिग्मकरे जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥६॥
अयि निजहुङ्कृतिमात्रनिराकृतधूम्रविलोचनधूम्रशते समरविशोषितशोणितबीजसमुद्भवशोणितबीजलते।
शिवशिवशुम्भनिशुम्भमहाहवतर्पितभूतपिशाचरते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥७॥
धनुरनुसंगरणक्षणसंगपरिस्फुरदङ्गनटत्कटके कनकपिशङ्गपृषत्कनिषङ्गरसद्भटशृङ्गहताबटुके।
कृतचतुरंगबलक्षितिरङ्गघटद्बहुरङ्गरटद्बटुके जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥८॥
सुरललना-ततथेयि-तथेयि-कृताभिनयोदर-नृत्यरते कृतकुकुथः कुकुथो गडदादिक-ताल-कुतूहल-गानरते।
धुधुकुट धुक्कुट धिंधिमितध्वनिधीरमृदङ्गनिनादरते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्यकपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥९॥
जय-जय-जप्य-जयेजयशब्द-परस्तुति-तत्परविश्वनुते झण-झण-झिञ्झिमि झिङ्कृत नूपुरसिंजितमोहित भूतपते।
नटितनटार्ध नटी नट नायक नाटितनाट्य सुगानरते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१०॥
अयि सुमनः सुमनः सुमनः सुमनः सुमनोहरकांतियुते श्रितरजनी-रजनीरजनी-रजनीरजनीकर-वक्त्रवृते।
सुनयनविभ्रमर-भ्रमरभ्रमर-भ्रमरभ्रमराधिपते।
जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥११॥
सहितमहाहव-मल्लमतल्लिक-मल्लितरल्लक-मल्लरते विरचितवल्लिक-पल्लिकमल्लिक-भिल्लिकभिल्लिक-वर्गवृते।
सित्कृत्पुल्लसमुल्लसितारुण-तल्लज-पल्लव-सल्ललिते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१२॥
अविरलगण्ड-गलन्मदमेदुर-मत्तमत्तंगज-राजपते त्रिभिवनभूषणभूत-कलानिधि-रूपपयोनिधि-राजसुते।
अयि सुदतीजन-लालसमानस-मोहनमन्मथराजसुते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१३॥
कमलदलामल-कोमलकान्ति-कला-कलितामल-भाललते सकलविलास-कलानिलयक्रम-केलिचलत्कल-हंसकुले।
अलिकुलसङ्कुल-कुवलयमण्डल-मौलिमिलद्बकुलालिकुले जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१४॥
करमुरलीरव-वीजितकूजित-लज्जितकोकिल-मञ्जुमते मिलितपुलिन्द-मनोहरगुंजित-रंजितशैल-निकुञ्जगते।
निजगुणभूत-महाशबरीगण-सद्गुणसम्भृत-केलितले जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१५॥
कटितटपीत-दुकूलविचित्र-मयूखतिरस्कृत-चन्द्ररुचे प्रणतसुरासुर-मौलिमणिस्फुरदंशुल-सन्नख-चन्द्ररुचे।
जितकनकाचल-मौलिपदोर्जित-निर्भरकुंजर-कुम्भकुचे जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१६॥
विजितसहस्र-करैक-सहस्र-करैक-सहस्र-करैकनुते कृतसुरतारक-सङ्गरतारक-सङ्गरतारक-सुनूसुते।
सुरथसमाधि-समानसमाधि-समाधि-समाधि-सुजातरते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१७॥
पदकमलं करुणानिलये वरिवस्यति योनुदिनम् स शिवे अयि कमले कमलानिलये कमलानिलयः स कथं न भवेत्।
तव पदमेव परम्पदमित्यनुशीलयतो मम किं न शिवे जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१८॥
कनकलसत्कलसिन्धु-जलैरनु-सिञ्चिनुते गुणरङ्गभुवम् भजति स किं न शचीकुचकुम्भतटीपरिरम्भ-सुखानुभवम्।
तवचरणं शरणङ्करवाणि नतामरवाणिनिवासिशिवम् जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥१९॥
तव विमलेन्दुकुलं वदनेन्दुमलं सकलं ननुकूलयते किमु पुरुहूतपुरीन्दु-मुखी-सुमुखीभिरसौ विमुखीक्रियते।
मम तु मतं शिवनामधने भवती कृपया किमुत क्रियते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥२०॥
अयि मयि दीन दयालुतया कृपयैव त्वया भवितव्यमुमे अयि जगतो जननी कृपयासि यथासि तथानुमितासिरते।
यदुचितमत्र भवत्युररी-कुरुतादुरुतापमपाकुरुते जय जय हे महिषासुरमर्दिनि रम्य कपर्दिनि शैलसुते॥२१॥
स्तुतिमिमां स्तिमितः सुसमाधिना नियमतो यमतोनुदिनं पठेत्।
परमया रमया स निषेव्यते परिजनोऽरिजनोऽपि च तं भजेत् ॥
O daughter of the mountain, who gladdens the earth, who delights the universe, praised by Nandi, who dwells on the summit of the great Vindhya mountain, who delights with Vishnu, praised by Indra,
O goddess, consort of the blue-throated one, of the vast family, of many deeds, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 1

Who showers blessings on the best of gods, who assails the unassailable Durdhara, who endures the foul-faced Durmukha, who delights in joy, who nourishes the three worlds, who pleases Shankara, who steals away sin, who delights in the battle-cry,

who rages at the sons of Danu, who is wrathful at the sons of Diti, who dries up the arrogant, daughter of the ocean, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 2
O mother of the world, my mother, who loves to dwell in the kadamba grove, who delights in laughter, who stays in your own home on the peak of the lofty Himalaya, crest-jewel of the mountains [?],

sweet as honey, who humbled Madhu and Kaitabha, who shattered Kaitabha, who delights in the round dance, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 3

O you who cut into a hundred pieces the lord of elephants, his body headless, his trunk hacked away [?]; whose lion, lord of beasts, is fierce in valour, tearing open the temples of the enemy's elephants [?],

who with the rod of your own arm struck down the lord of the warriors, felled in pieces, his head cut off [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 4
O bearer of the irresistible, unaging power [?] raised to slay the enemies maddened by battle, who made the lord of the Pramathas, the great Shiva, foremost in clever counsel, your messenger,

whose mind was death to the envoy [?] of the demons, sinful, evil in wish, evil in purpose, evil in thought, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 5

O you whose hand grants fearlessness to the wives of enemies and to the best of their heroes who come to you for refuge [?], whose hand holds the spotless trident, laid on the neck of the foe who was a spike in the head of the three worlds,

who made the hot-rayed sun resound with the great sound [?] of the gods' drums beating dumi-dumi, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 6
O you who by your mere cry of hum drove away Dhumralochana and his hundreds of smoke-grey ones [?], who in battle dried up the creeper [?] of Raktabija sprung from Raktabija's blood,

who delight in the ghosts and goblins sated in the great battle with Shumbha and Nishumbha, Shiva, Shiva [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 7
whose bracelets dance on your limbs, quivering as you cling to the bow at every moment of battle, who struck down the foremost [?] of the warriors loud with their quivers of gold-tawny arrows [?],

who made the fourfold army [?] on the stage of the earth, where troops of many colours clash and young warriors [?] cry out, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 8
who delight in the dance of the women of the gods, rich in gesture, beaten out as tatatheyi, tatheyi, who delight in songs that play with rhythms, kukutha, kukutha, gadada and the like,

who delight in the sound of the mridanga drum, deep with the ring of dhudhukuta, dhukkuta, dhim-dhim, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 9

praised by the whole world, intent on the highest praise, with cries of jaya, jaya to be chanted and of victory, victory, you who enchanted the lord of beings with the jingling of your anklets, jhana-jhana, jhinjhimi [?],

O half of the Dancer who danced [?], dancer, actor, leading player [?], who delight in drama staged and in sweet song, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 10
O flower, flower, good-minded, good-minded [?], endowed with a radiance that charms the good-minded, whose face, resting on night, night, night, is like the moon, maker of night [?],
whose lovely eyes rove like bees, bees, bees, O queen of the bees [?],
victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 11
who delight in the finest of wrestlers, met in the great battle [?], surrounded by a company of Bhil women decked with creepers and jasmine [?],
graceful as the finest young red shoots, blossoming and shining [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 12

O you [who move like] the king of elephants, rutting and wild, thick with the ichor flowing ceaselessly from its temples [?], daughter of the king, the ocean, whose form is the moon, store of beauty, an ornament of the three worlds [?],

O daughter of the king [?], [like] Manmatha who bewitches minds full of longing for fair-toothed women [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 13

whose spotless forehead is adorned with a soft radiance, spotless as a lotus petal, and with the crescent [?], [whose gait is like] a flock of swans moving sweetly in play, the home of every grace and art [?],

on whose crown the bakula flowers and swarms of bees meet, among rings of blue water-lilies crowded with bees, victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 14
lovely-minded one, the sound of the flute in your hand putting to shame the cuckoo's song [?], who go to the mountain bowers made glad by the charming humming of the gathered Pulindas,

whose playground is filled with the good qualities of the great band of Shabara women, born of your own qualities [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 15

whose bright-patterned yellow silk at the hips outshines the moon's light with its rays, whose fine toenails shine like moons, lit by the rays flashing from the crest-jewels of the gods and demons bowing down,

whose breasts, full like the temple-domes of elephants, surpass the peak of the golden mountain [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 16

praised by the one who conquered thousands with a single hand, by the thousand-rayed one, by the thousand-handed one [?], whose son was the deliverer in the battle with Taraka, born to deliver the gods [?],

who delight in Suratha and Samadhi, in their like meditation, meditation upon meditation, and in the well-born [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 17
O home of compassion, he who worships your lotus feet day after day, O auspicious one, O Kamala, who dwell in the lotus, how should he not become a home of Kamala?

As I keep in mind that your feet alone are the highest state, what should not be mine, O auspicious one? Victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 18
He who sprinkles the ground, the stage of your virtues [?], with the waters of the river shining with gold [?], does he not know the joy of embracing the jar-like breasts of Shachi?

Let me make your feet my refuge, the auspicious [feet] where dwell the gods who bow and Vani [?]. Victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 19
Your face, a moon, spotless moon of the moon's spotless race [?], wholly draws one to the shore [?]; is he then turned away by the moon-faced, fair-faced women of Indra's city [?]?

But my thought is this, O you whose wealth is the name of Shiva [?]: what is not done by your grace? Victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 20
O Uma, to me, wretched, you must be kind out of compassion and grace alone; O mother of the world, as you are in your compassion, so you are known, O you who delight [?],
whatever is fitting here, may you accept it; you who take away great torment [?], victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon, of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain. 21
Whoever, still, in deep concentration, with restraint and discipline, recites this hymn of praise day after day,
he is attended by Ramā, supreme Fortune, and his own people, and even his enemies, shall honour him.

suralalanā-tatatheyi-tatheyi-kṛtābhinayodara-nṛtyarate kṛtakukuthaḥ kukutho gaḍadādika-tāla-kutūhala-gānarate |

notes: Verses 1 and 2: the English is the site owner's own translation, divided between the two half-verses.
Romanization: IAST, of the text as printed, including its spelling of anusvara (śaṃkara, kāṃti, guṃjita) and its word divisions and hyphens; | and || stand for the danda and double danda.

Refrain (every verse): jaya jaya he mahiṣāsuramardini ramya kapardini śailasute, 'victory, victory to you, slayer of the buffalo demon (Mahishasura), of lovely braided hair, daughter of the mountain'. Kapardin, 'wearing the braided coil of hair', is otherwise an epithet of Shiva. Verse 9 prints ramyakapardini as one word.

line 1.1: the text prints nandanute, 'praised by Nanda' (or 'praised with joy'); the usual reading is nandinute, 'praised by Nandi', which the owner's translation follows. 'Who delights with Vishnu' (viṣṇuvilāsini) and 'praised by Indra' (jiṣṇunute: jiṣṇu, 'the victorious', is a name of Indra, also of Vishnu and Arjuna).
line 1.2: śitikaṇṭha, 'the blue-throated one', is Shiva.
line 2.1: Durdhara and Durmukha are demons named in the Devi Mahatmya; the words also mean 'the unbearable' and 'the foul-mouthed'. The text prints durmukhamarṣiṇī with a long final ī.
line 2.2: sindhusute, 'daughter of the ocean', is a name of Lakshmi, who rose from the churned ocean.
line 3.1: śikhariśiromaṇi, 'crest-jewel of the mountains', may describe the Himalaya rather than the goddess.
line 3.2: Madhu and Kaitabha are the two demons slain at the beginning of the Devi Mahatmya; rāsa is the circle dance.

line 4: the long compounds are uncertain. The -adhipate endings ('O lord of …') are read here as describing the goddess through her deeds and her lion; śuṇḍamṛgādhipate ('lord of beasts', the lion) has an unclear first member, and muṇḍa ('shaven head', 'head') may be the demon Munda.

line 5.1: nirjara is 'unaging' and also 'a god'; the compound may mean 'bearer of the gods' irresistible power'. In the Devi Mahatmya the goddess sends Shiva as her messenger to the demons, hence Shivaduti.
line 5.2: dūta ('envoy') in this compound is uncertain; the sense may be simply 'whose mind is death to the demons'.

line 6.1: śūla is both 'spike, trident' and 'sharp pain': the foe was a pain in the head of the three worlds. The first compound, granting fearlessness to enemies' wives and heroes who take refuge, is uncertain in its parts.
line 6.2: dumi-dumi imitates the drum; the text prints nādamaho as a separate word, read here as 'great sound' (mahas, 'splendour, festival', is also possible).

line 7.1: hum is the goddess's cry of anger. Dhumralochana ('smoke-eyed') is a demon; dhūmraśate may be 'a hundred smoke-grey ones' or 'a hundred Dhumras'. Śoṇitabīja is Raktabija ('blood-seed'), from each drop of whose blood a new demon sprang; latā 'creeper' may mean that spreading brood.
line 7.2: śiva-śiva may be an exclamation or 'auspicious, auspicious'. Bhūtas and piśācas are ghosts and goblins.

line 8: very uncertain. hatābaṭuke may be read hata-abaṭuke or hatā baṭuke; baṭuka is 'a boy, a youth' (also a form of Bhairava). caturaṃgabala is the fourfold army of chariots, elephants, horse and foot.
lines 9.1-9.2: tatatheyi, kukutha, gaḍada, dhudhukuṭa and dhiṃdhimi are dance and drum syllables, kept as sounds. The mridanga is a two-headed drum.
line 10.1: bhūtapati, 'lord of beings', is Shiva; the phrase may mean that she enchanted him or that the world-lord is enchanted. jhaṇa, jhiñjhimi imitate the anklets.
line 10.2: naṭārdha, 'half of the Dancer', alludes to Shiva the dancer and to the goddess as his half; the string naṭī naṭa nāyaka ('dancer, actor, leader') is uncertain in construction.

line 11: the verse is a play of sounds that cannot be carried over: sumanas means 'flower', 'good-minded', 'a god'; rajanī is 'night' (and turmeric), rajanīkara 'maker of night', the moon; bhramara is 'bee' and bhramarādhipate may refer to the goddess as Bhramari, of the bees. The translation follows the words, not a settled sense.

line 12: very uncertain. malla is 'wrestler', matallikā 'the best of its kind'; bhillikā are Bhil women, a forest people; mallikā is jasmine. The text prints sitkṛt- at the start of 12.2, where other copies have sitakṛta ('made white').

line 13.1: the text prints tribhivana for tribhuvana ('three worlds'). kalānidhi, 'store of digits (or arts)', is the moon; the moon and Lakshmi both rose from the ocean, 'the king, the ocean'. The comparison with the elephant king is supplied in brackets.
line 13.2: manmatharājasute is literally 'daughter of king Manmatha' (Manmatha, 'mind-churner', is Kama, the god of love); the sense is disputed.
line 14: the brackets supply the comparison usual in such verses (the goddess's gait like swans). bakula is the Mimusops elengi tree, its flowers worn in the hair.
line 15: Pulindas and Shabaras are forest and hill peoples of the Sanskrit texts. vījita ('fanned, surpassed') is uncertain.
line 16.2: kanakācala, 'the golden mountain', is Meru. The comparison of breasts to an elephant's temple-domes is a convention of Sanskrit poetry.

line 17.1: very uncertain. sahasrakara is 'thousand-rayed' (the sun) and 'thousand-handed'; tāraka is 'deliverer' and the demon Taraka, slain by the goddess's son Skanda (Kartikeya). The text prints sunūsute (sūnu, 'son').
line 17.2: Suratha (a king) and Samadhi (a merchant) are the two listeners to whom the Devi Mahatmya is told; samādhi is also 'deep meditation', and the line plays on both.

line 18.1: kamalānilaya is 'dwelling in the lotus' and 'a home of Kamala' (Lakshmi, prosperity); śive, 'O auspicious one', is also a name of Shiva's consort. The text prints yonudinam without the avagraha (yo 'nudinam).
line 19.1: siñcinute is an unusual form, perhaps anusiñcati te, 'sprinkles … for you'. Shachi is the wife of Indra; the joy of embracing her is Indra's bliss, the reward of heaven.
line 19.2: natāmaravāṇinivāsi, 'where the bowing gods and Vani (Sarasvati, speech) dwell', is uncertain.
line 20.1: the sense of the half-verse is disputed; the words may also be divided vadanendum alaṃ sakalaṃ nanu kūlayate. Puruhūta, 'much invoked', is Indra; his city is heaven.
line 20.2: śivanāmadhane may also mean 'O you who are named Shiva's treasure'.
line 21.1: Uma is a name of Parvati. anumitāsirate is unclear: anumitā asi rate ('you are inferred, O delighting one') or asirate ('who delight in the sword').

lines 22-23: the closing verses (phala-shruti), in a different metre, state the reward of reciting the hymn. They play on paramayā ramayā ('by the supreme Rama', i.e. Lakshmi, fortune) and parijana / arijana ('his own people' / 'his enemies'); yamata(ḥ) and niyamata(ḥ) are 'with restraint' and 'with discipline'. The text prints yamatonudinaṃ without the avagraha.
line 23.1: Ramā is Lakshmi, the goddess of fortune, not the god Rama.
